newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian racism row seen threatening Asia trade.
newsitem.headline: Australian racism row seen threatening Asia trade.

text.p: Australian industry groups called on the government on Wednesday to take a decisive stand on racial intolerance, saying they were concerned the country's heated racism debate could damage trade ties with Asia.

Racism and racial issues have dominated the news for a month since independent politician Pauline Hanson criticised the government over the number of Asian immigrants in Australia and hinted at an Asian invasion threat.

"The comments can only be construed as inflammatory and certainly must run the risk of damaging trade if they're allowed to go unchecked," the executive director of the Australian Council of Wool Exporters, Bob Quirk, told Reuters.

Prime Minister John Howard has been criticised for his failure to openly condemn Hanson's remarks. Howard told reporters on Wednesday the row would already have blown over had it not been for incessant media attention.
"My view is that the remarks made by the member for Oxley have been ridiculously given prominence," Howard said.
But industry and trade groups said Howard should have actively distanced himself from Hanson's remarks rather than let the damaging debate linger on.
"The comments, if left unchallenged by the prime minister, certainly have the potential to damage trade," said Ian MacFarlane, president of the Grains Council of Australia.
MacFarlane told Reuters the council had already received a "steady stream of concerns" from its trading partners, although there was no evidence trade had yet suffered.
Howard said on Tuesday he would hold discussions with the opposition over a proposed bi-partisan motion against racial intolerance -- a move that MacFarlane said was urgently needed.
"We just need to make sure that there's no confusion in the Asians' minds as to where the government and ourselves stand on this," MacFarlane said.
"Whether John Howard supports the opposition motion or whether he just supports the contents of it in principle, we would be satisfied."
Quirk also welcomed the move, but said the government could have acted far more quickly to neutralise the debate.
"To me, it's an issue that should never have been allowed to go this far," Quirk said.

"I think the government could have marginalised or done quite a lot more to make it quite clear that Hanson's comments in no way reflect the overwhelming Australian view and certainly not that of the government."

Earlier this month, Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer warned that Hanson's anti-Asian statements may have already affected trade with the region. However, industry groups said trade remained largely unaffected at this point.
"All we're getting back from them is queries about where the debate is going," MacFarlane said. "I suspect, though, that they are watching the situation very closely."
Tourism Council Australia said it would be three to six months before it would know if the debate was affecting tourism.

"But the industry is certainly worried about the perception that these sort of comments create particularly in Asian countries, which of course are obviously a huge growth market for Australian tourism," spokeswoman Jenny Stevenson said.
